question: What is a Python module?
correct: A file of Python code that other files can import and use
incorrect: A block of code that repeats until a condition becomes false
A single value stored under a name inside a function
A message Python prints when your program has an error
feedback: A module is just a file of code. Python ships with hundreds of them — the standard library — and any file you write can be imported the same way.

question: What does the line  import math  let you do?
correct: Use the tools inside math by writing math.sqrt(...) and math.pi
incorrect: Use sqrt(...) directly with no prefix in front of it
Copy the math module's code into your file permanently
Convert the numbers in your program into decimals
feedback: import math brings the whole module into reach, and the dot means 'look inside'. To use a name bare, you would write from math import sqrt instead.

question: What is the difference between  import random  and  from random import choice?
correct: The first requires the random. prefix; the second lets you call choice directly
incorrect: The first loads the module faster than the second does
The first works inside functions, the second at the top of a file
The first imports the module once, the second re-imports on each call
feedback: Both reach the same code. The from form is shorter to type; the plain import keeps it obvious where a name came from, which matters in a long file.

question: Merlin's team has nine copies of the same fee-calculating code, and three of them have different bugs. Which change fixes the underlying problem?
correct: Put the fee function in one module and import it everywhere it is needed
incorrect: Fix the nine copies carefully and add a comment to each one
Rename the copies so it is clear which one is the newest
Move the nine copies together into one very long file
feedback: One definition, many imports. Copies drift apart no matter how careful people are, so the fix is to have only one place where the rule lives.

question: Guinevere tracks citizens in four parallel lists (names, ages, wards, balances) lined up by position. What is the main danger of this design?
correct: Sorting or inserting into one list silently misaligns it from the others
incorrect: Python limits a program to three lists at the same time
Lists refuse to hold text and numbers in one program
Reading from four lists uses four times as much memory
feedback: The lists are held together only by the fragile promise that index 0 means the same person in all four. One object per citizen keeps each person's facts together instead.

question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
correct: A class is the blueprint; an object is one thing built from that blueprint
incorrect: A class holds the data while an object holds the methods
A class belongs to Python while an object is written by you
A class runs immediately while an object waits to be called
feedback: One Citizen class can stamp out thousands of citizen objects, each with its own name, ward, and balance. The blueprint is shared; the data is not.

question: When does a class's  __init__  method run?
correct: Automatically, each time a new object is built from the class
incorrect: When you call it by name, as object.__init__()
Once when the class definition is first read by Python
Each time one of the object's other methods is called
feedback: __init__ is the setup routine. Writing Citizen("Elaine", "North", 120.0) runs it immediately, and its parameters line up with the arguments you passed.

question:
What does this program print?

class Citizen:
    def __init__(self, name, balance):
        self.name = name
        self.balance = balance

elaine = Citizen("Elaine", 120)
percival = Citizen("Percival", 40)
elaine.balance = elaine.balance + 50
print(percival.balance)
feedback: Each object gets its own copy of the data set up in __init__, so changing elaine's balance leaves percival's alone. The class is shared; the instance data is not.

question: In a method definition such as  def pay(self, amount):, what does  self  refer to?
correct: The particular object the method was called on
incorrect: The class itself, rather than any one object
The value the method is going to return
A required name for the method's first real argument
feedback: When you write elaine.pay(20), Python fills self with elaine and amount with 20. That is why the call passes one argument but the definition lists two.

correct: Without self. it creates a local variable that disappears when the method ends
incorrect: The subtraction happens before the assignment is allowed
A method is unable to change data that __init__ created
The method is missing a return statement at the end
feedback: Bare balance is a throwaway local name. The fix is one word: self.balance = self.balance - amount. When an update mysteriously does not stick, check for a missing self. first.

question: A function defined inside a class, which acts on that object's own data, is called a ___.
correct: method
feedback: A method is just a function that lives inside a class and takes self as its first parameter.

question: What is an attribute?
correct: A piece of data stored on an object, such as self.name
incorrect: The name of the class an object was built from
A parameter listed in a method's definition line
A module imported at the top of the file
feedback: Attributes are the facts an object carries. You set them with self.name = name inside __init__ and read them back with elaine.name.

question: Why does a leading underscore, as in  self._pin, matter in Python?
correct: It is a convention telling other programmers the value is internal, not a lock
incorrect: It makes Python refuse any access from outside the class
It encrypts the value to stop it being printed by mistake
It tells Python to delete the value when the method ends
feedback: Python has no hard privacy. The underscore is a message to humans: reach this through a method such as check_pin() rather than touching it directly. That discipline is encapsulation.

question: What does defining a  __str__  method on a class change?
correct: What is displayed when an object is printed
incorrect: The name Python uses for the class internally
Whether the object's attributes can be edited
The order in which the object's methods run
feedback: Without __str__, printing an object shows something like <__main__.Account object at 0x...>. With it, you decide the text — and you can leave sensitive fields out of it.

question: What does the line  class Knight(Guard):  mean?
correct: Knight inherits Guard's attributes and methods, and can add or change its own
incorrect: Knight stores a Guard object inside each knight
Knight and Guard are two names for the very same class
Guard is passed as an argument each time a Knight is built
feedback: The parentheses mark inheritance: Guard is the parent, Knight is the child. Even an empty Knight body already has everything Guard defined.

question: In a child class's  __init__, what does  super().__init__(name)  do?
correct: Runs the parent's setup for the shared data, so the child need not retype it
incorrect: Creates a separate parent object stored inside the child
Replaces the parent's setup with the child's version
Copies the parent class definition into the child class
feedback: super() refers to the parent class. Calling its __init__ handles the shared fields, and then the child adds only what is new to it.

correct: Sir Lancelot leads the patrol.
incorrect: Lancelot is on patrol.
An error, because Knight has no __init__
Sir Lancelot is on patrol.
feedback: Knight inherits __init__ from Guard, so the name is stored. Knight also defines its own patrol, which overrides the parent's version for knight objects.

question: Defining a method in a child class with the same name as the parent's, so the child's version wins, is called an ___.
correct: override
feedback: Overriding lets a child specialise one behaviour while keeping everything else it inherited.

question: A list holds a mix of Guard and Knight objects, and a loop calls  officer.patrol()  on each without checking their types. Which idea makes this work?
correct: Polymorphism — each object runs the version of patrol belonging to its own class
incorrect: Encapsulation — the objects hide their data from the loop
Composition — the list contains the objects rather than inheriting them
Abstraction — the loop is written at a higher level than the objects
feedback: One method name, many behaviours, chosen automatically by the object. Add a new kind of officer tomorrow and this loop keeps working untouched — no if-statement to update.

question: You are deciding between inheritance and composition. Which of these are best modelled as "is-a" relationships, suited to inheritance? (Select all that apply)
correct: A Knight and a Guard
A LeadResearcher and a Researcher
incorrect: A Squad and the guards it contains
A Study and its list of participants
A DispatchDesk and the packages waiting on it
feedback: A knight is a kind of guard, so inheritance fits. A squad is not a kind of guard — it has guards, which is composition. When one thing merely contains another, store it rather than inherit from it.

question: Why is  members = []  written directly in a class body a bug when each object should have its own list?
correct: There is one list shared by every object, so adding through one shows up in all
incorrect: Python forbids a list from appearing inside a class body
The list is deleted as soon as the first object is created
Each object gets a list, but the lists are locked as read-only
feedback: Anything that should differ between objects belongs in __init__ as self.members = []. This is the OOP cousin of the aliasing trap: one object, many names pointing at it.

question: Match each of the four pillars of object-oriented programming to its description.

pairs.definition: Bundling data with the methods that guard it
Hiding the how behind a simple interface
Letting a child class build on a parent
One method name behaving correctly per object

feedback: Being able to name these four and give an example of each is what it means to understand object-oriented design.

question: Using the noun/verb heuristic on a problem description, what do the nouns and verbs suggest?
correct: Nouns suggest classes and attributes; verbs suggest methods
incorrect: Nouns suggest methods; verbs suggest classes and attributes
Nouns suggest modules; verbs suggest the imports they need
Nouns suggest parameters; verbs suggest their default values
feedback: Write the problem in plain English, then underline. 'A courier picks up a package' gives classes Courier and Package, and a method pick_up. It will not hand you a perfect design, but it gets you off the blank page.

question: A class tracks packages, couriers, billing, and the weather. Which design idea does it violate?
correct: Cohesion — a class should have one clear responsibility
incorrect: Coupling — a class should not talk to any other class
Inheritance — a class ought to extend some parent class
Encapsulation — a class should hold at most one attribute
feedback: That class has low cohesion: four unrelated jobs in one box. The design goal is high cohesion (each class minds one job) and low coupling (changing one class does not force rewrites elsewhere).

question: Two classes are tightly coupled. What does that mean in practice?
correct: Changing one of them tends to force changes in the other
incorrect: They are stored in the same Python module file
One of them inherits each method from the other
They both create objects at the same point in the program
feedback: Tight coupling makes a program fragile: a small edit ripples outward. Classes that talk only through a few clean methods stay independent and safe to change.

question: Nimue's  DeliveryQueue  stores packages in a list but exposes only  enqueue,  dequeue, and  is_empty. What does that buy her?
correct: She can change the internal storage later without touching any code that uses the queue
incorrect: The queue runs faster than it would if the list were public
Other programmers are prevented by Python from reading the list
The queue can hold more packages than a plain list could
feedback: Callers depend only on the promise — the method names — not the storage. That separation of interface from implementation is exactly the ADT idea, now built as a class.

question: The course describes a tower of abstraction layers. Which ordering matches it, from lowest to highest?
correct: Transistors, logic gates, machine code, Python, your classes
incorrect: Python, machine code, logic gates, transistors, your classes
Your classes, Python, transistors, logic gates, machine code
Logic gates, transistors, Python, machine code, your classes
feedback: Each layer hides the mess below it. That is how a small mind builds a large machine: you write a class without ever thinking about transistors.

question:
What does this program print?

class Squad:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.members = []
    def recruit(self, guard):
        self.members.append(guard)

watch = Squad("Night Watch")
watch.recruit("Gareth")
watch.recruit("Lancelot")
print(len(watch.members))
incorrect: "Night Watch"
feedback: Because self.members is created inside __init__, this squad has its own list. Two recruits were appended, so its length is 2.

question: Which of these describe object-oriented programming rather than procedural programming? (Select all that apply)
correct: Data and the behaviour that acts on it travel together in one bundle
An object changes its own data through its own methods
incorrect: Data sits in variables while separate functions reach out and change it
Programs are written without ever defining a function
Values in the program are restricted to whole numbers
feedback: Procedural code has passive data and bossy functions. OOP flips that: each object owns its data and its behaviour, which is what keeps large programs from tangling.

question: Write the Python header line that begins a class named Guard with no parent class.
correct: class Guard:
feedback: A class header is the keyword class, the name in CapWords, and a colon. A parent, if any, goes in parentheses: class Knight(Guard):

question: Inside a method, write the Python statement that stores the parameter  n  onto the object as an attribute called n.
correct: self.n = n
feedback: self.name = name puts the value on the object, so it travels with that object. Leaving off self. would create a local variable that vanishes.

question: Building an object out of other objects, a "has-a" relationship rather than an "is-a" one, is called ___.
correct: composition
feedback: A famous guideline says to favour composition over inheritance: you can change what an object contains while the program runs, but you cannot change a class's parent.
